svg.title: How Kapitsa works: DFlash2 vs KFlash
svg.desc: DFlash2 vs KFlash, side by side, above three cards. DFlash2, the drafter's chain: one chain, as Splash, oMLX and mlx-serve run it. The drafter guesses the next 7 tokens. The big model checks them in one pass and keeps them up to the first wrong guess. Example: the chain return a - b gets two checks and a cross, so return and a are kept and the rest is dropped: 1 pass, 2 tokens. KFlash, Kapitsa's: a best-first tree from the same drafters, no retraining. In the same one pass, the big model checks a best-first tree of the drafter's top candidates in 8 rows. Where the drafter is unsure, its runner-up guesses ride along, and the longest branch the big model agrees with is kept. Example: return a, then a branch - or +; - is wrong and + b is kept: 8 rows, 1 pass, 4 tokens. Same output as plain decoding. Tree size measured on each Mac. +8-17% more tokens per pass on short prompts (M4 Pro). 4B: +8% decode (T 0.6), +10% greedy. GPU, hand-written Metal code: every layer runs on GPU code made for these exact models and for Apple silicon, not a general-purpose framework (every layer, every token). Neural Engine, helps read long prompts: on the 4B, 27B, Bolt and Super-VL it reads part of each prompt beside the GPU (one prompt, two chips). Memory, keeps conversations ready: each conversation keeps what it has already read, so a follow-up only reads the new message. Up to 4 at once (up to 4 kept warm).
